newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian coalition divided over Aboriginal land.
newsitem.headline: Australian coalition divided over Aboriginal land.

text.p: Australia's National Party stepped up pressure on Prime Minister John Howard on Monday to protect farmers from Aboriginal land claims, an issue that is threatening to split the ruling coalition.
Deputy prime minister and Nationals leader Tim Fischer said he would seek cabinet approval at a meeting on Tuesday for the government to legislate supremacy for farm leases over Aboriginal claims.
"We can afford nothing less. Indeed, we must look at the whole land title structure because that is what is in jeopardy," Fischer told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.

"The leafy suburbs of Sydney and Melbourne can afford nothing less. You cannot have a defective land titles system across the majority of the land of Australia, whilst of course retaining the right for provision of native title on vacant Crown (government) land."

The government is due soon to announce its response to a December High Court ruling, known as the Wik decision, that leases granted to farmers since white settlers arrived more than 200 years ago did not automatically wipe out "native title".
Native title rights were granted to Aborigines three years ago by the former Labor government but the relationship between Aboriginal claims and pastoral leases was left ill-defined.

Already over a third of Australian land is being claimed by indigenous Aborigines and the premier of the northern state of Queensland, the National Party's Rob Borbidge, has said 85 percent of the state could be hit by claims.

Fischer's rural-based party, the junior member of Howard's conservative coalition, is under pressure in its heartland to protect farmers from native title claims and Borbidge has threatened to sever ties with Howard over the issue.

National Party members of the the federal government, complaining of Liberal bullying over a range of issues, have also threatened to walk out of the coalition, although Howard's Liberal Party has the numbers to govern on its own.
Howard has said he wanted a negotiated compromise, satisfying Aboriginal and farm groups, but would impose his own settlement if no compromise could be struck.
Farm groups say the Wik ruling created uncertainty about what they can do with their land and jeopardised rural industry.

The uncertainty extends to mining and exploration on pastoral land. Queensland said last month it had frozen about 500 mining exploration applications until the issue of land tenure security was settled.
But Howard has been warned almost any decision, including outright extinguishment of Aboriginal rights, could spark massive compensation claims from either Aborigines or farmers.
The government has also been warned any decision must not breach its own laws against racial discrimination.
Borbidge said he was cautiously optimistic that Howard would legislate to extinguish native title on pastoral leases.
"I don't expect a final decision from the federal government this week, but what I do expect is a progress report from the prime minister," he said.
One option would be to allow Aboriginal and pastoral rights to co-exist, but give the pastoral lease supremacy if there was conflict.
